summary: Defines an extensible way to return extra information about why a DNS error occurred. It was created mainly to extend SERVFAIL with details about DNS and DNSSEC failures, but any response type can carry extended error information. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a DNS lookup fails, the reply usually says only that it failed. RFC 8914 lets the server attach a reason, as a numbered code plus optional text: the answer failed signature validation, the name is on a blocklist, the server could not reach the authoritative server, and so on. The reason is for diagnostics and must not change how the lookup is handled.

subtitle: A way for DNS servers to say why a query failed, not just that it failed.

tldr.problem: A DNS server has very few ways to report failure. A SERVFAIL does not say whether the answer failed DNSSEC validation, whether the name is on a blocklist, or whether the server simply could not reach the authoritative server, so applications and resolvers have to guess.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8914 adds an EDNS0 option, code 15, that carries a 16-bit error code and optional human-readable text. The codes form a registry that covers DNSSEC validation failures, policy blocks, operational failures and stale cached answers.
tldr.outcome: A resolver or application that receives the option knows why the lookup failed, and can decide whether to try another server, warn the user, or log something useful. The information is diagnostic only and must not change how DNS is processed. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8914 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2020, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the Extended DNS Error EDNS0 option and the registry of error codes, and it is built on the EDNS0 mechanism of RFC 6891.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
There are many reasons a DNS query may fail: some are transient and some permanent; some can be resolved by querying another server, and some are best handled by stopping resolution. Unfortunately, the error signals a DNS server can return are very limited and not very expressive. Applications and resolvers often have to guess at the issue. Was the answer marked REFUSED because of a lame delegation, or because the nameserver is still starting up and loading zones? Is a SERVFAIL a DNSSEC validation issue, or is the nameserver experiencing some other failure? What error message should be presented to the user or logged in these conditions?

Errors caused by DNSSEC validation issues are a good example of what would benefit from more information. When a stub resolver queries a name that is DNSSEC bogus, using a validating resolver, the stub resolver receives only a SERVFAIL. The SERVFAIL Response Code is used to signal many sorts of DNS errors, so the stub resolver's only option is to ask the next configured DNS resolver. The result is one of two outcomes: either the next resolver also validates and a SERVFAIL is returned again, or the next resolver is not a validating resolver and the user is returned a potentially harmful result.

With an Extended DNS Error option enclosed in the response message, the resolver is able to return a more descriptive reason for why a failure happened, or to add additional context to a message containing a NOERROR RCODE. The Extended DNS Error codes described here can be used by any system that sends DNS queries and receives a response containing an EDE option. Different codes are useful in different circumstances, so different systems, such as stub resolvers, recursive resolvers and authoritative resolvers, might receive and use them.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS has one blunt failure code, and it means many different things. That is not just inconvenient for people reading logs. It makes a client behave badly: a stub resolver that gets SERVFAIL cannot tell whether the answer was rejected on security grounds, so it tries the next server, which may not validate at all.

sections.title: The Extended DNS Error Option
sections.content:
The document uses an Extended Mechanism for DNS option to include Extended DNS Error information in DNS messages. The option is structured as a 16-bit OPTION-CODE, a 16-bit OPTION-LENGTH, a 16-bit INFO-CODE, and a variable-length EXTRA-TEXT field.

OPTION-CODE is two octets, or 16 bits, as defined in RFC 6891, and contains the value 15 for EDE. OPTION-LENGTH is two octets and contains the length of the payload, everything after the length field itself, in octets; it should be 2 plus the length of the EXTRA-TEXT field, which may be a zero-length string. INFO-CODE is 16 bits and is the principal contribution of the document. This 16-bit value, encoded in network most significant bit byte order, provides the additional context for the RESPONSE-CODE of the DNS message, and serves as an index into the Extended DNS Errors registry.

EXTRA-TEXT is a variable-length, UTF-8-encoded text field that may hold additional textual information. The information is intended for human consumption, not automated parsing. EDE text may be null terminated but must not be assumed to be, and the length must be derived from the OPTION-LENGTH field. The field may be zero octets long, indicating that there is no EXTRA-TEXT included. Care should be taken not to include private information in the EXTRA-TEXT field that an observer would not otherwise have access to, such as account numbers.

The EDE option can be included in any response, whether SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, REFUSED or even NOERROR, to a query that includes an OPT pseudo-record. The document includes a set of initial codepoints but is extensible through the IANA registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The option rides in the extra section of a DNS message, next to the other extension fields. It holds a two-octet number that says which kind of failure it is, and optionally a line of text for a human to read. The text may be empty, and it must not be assumed to end with a null character, because its length comes from the option length field.

sections.title: Extended DNS Error Processing
sections.content:
When a response grows beyond the requestor's UDP payload size, servers should truncate messages by dropping EDE options before dropping other data from packets, and should set the truncation bit when dropping EDE options. Because long EXTRA-TEXT fields may trigger truncation, which is undesirable given the supplemental nature of EDE, implementers and operators creating EDE options should avoid lengthy EXTRA-TEXT contents.

When a resolver or forwarder receives an EDE option, whether and how to pass the information along to its original client is implementation dependent. Implementations may choose not to forward it, or may choose to create new EDE options that convey the information encoded in the received one. When doing so, the source of the error should be attributed in the EXTRA-TEXT field, since an EDNS0 option received by the original client will appear to have come from the resolver or forwarder that sent it.

The document does not allow or prohibit any particular extended error codes and information being matched with any particular RCODEs. Some combinations may seem nonsensical, such as resolver-specific extended error codes received in responses from authoritative servers, so systems interpreting the codes must not assume that a combination will make sense. Receivers must be able to accept EDE codes and EXTRA-TEXT in all messages, including those with a NOERROR RCODE, but need not act on them. Applications must continue to follow the requirements of applicable specifications on how to process RCODEs no matter what EDE values are also received. Senders may include more than one EDE option, and receivers must be able to accept, though not necessarily process or act on, multiple EDE options in a DNS message.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules matter for anyone building on this. The option must never change how a response is treated: the ordinary response code still decides what happens. And a middle server that rewrites the option should say where the error really came from, because the client will otherwise think the error came from it.

sections.title: Defined Extended DNS Errors
sections.content:
The document defines the initial set of EDE codes, from 0 to 24. The mechanism is intended to be extensible, and additional codepoints can be registered in the Extended DNS Errors registry.

Code 0, Other, covers an error that falls into no known category; implementations should include an EXTRA-TEXT value to augment it. Code 1, Unsupported DNSKEY Algorithm, means the resolver tried to validate but a DNSKEY RRset contained only unsupported DNSSEC algorithms. Code 2, Unsupported DS Digest Type, means the same for a DS RRset with only unsupported digest types.

Code 3, Stale Answer, means the resolver could not resolve within its time limits and answered with previously cached data instead of an error, typically because of problems communicating with an authoritative server, possibly as a result of a denial of service attack against another network. Code 4, Forged Answer, means an answer was forged for policy reasons, such as a legal obligation or malware filtering; it should be used when an answer is still provided, not when a failure code is returned instead.

Codes 5 to 12 cover DNSSEC validation. Code 5, DNSSEC Indeterminate, means validation ended in the Indeterminate state. Code 6, DNSSEC Bogus, means it ended in the Bogus state. Code 7, Signature Expired, means no signatures are presently valid and some, often all, are expired. Code 8, Signature Not Yet Valid, means no signatures are presently valid and at least some are not yet valid. Code 9, DNSKEY Missing, means a DS record existed at a parent but no supported matching DNSKEY record could be found for the child. Code 10, RRSIGs Missing, means no RRSIGs could be found for at least one RRset where they were expected. Code 11, No Zone Key Bit Set, means no Zone Key Bit was set in a DNSKEY. Code 12, NSEC Missing, means the requested data was missing and a covering NSEC or NSEC3 was not provided.

Code 13, Cached Error, means the resolver is returning the SERVFAIL RCODE from its cache. Code 14, Not Ready, means the server could not answer because it was not fully functional when the query was received.

Codes 15 to 18 cover policy decisions. Code 15, Blocked, means the server cannot respond because the domain is on a blocklist due to an internal security policy imposed by the operator of the server. Code 16, Censored, means the same but because of an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator; how the policy is applied, whether in-band filtering or a court order, is irrelevant. Code 17, Filtered, means the server cannot respond because the domain is on a blocklist as requested by the client. Code 18, Prohibited, is for an authoritative server or recursive resolver that receives a query from an unauthorized client, such as a recursive query from an IP address outside the network, a blocklisted address, or one that local policy forbids, and annotates its REFUSED message with the code.

Code 19, Stale NXDOMAIN Answer, means the resolver could not resolve an answer within its configured time limits and answered with a previously cached NXDOMAIN answer instead of an error. Code 20, Not Authoritative, is for an authoritative server that receives a query with the Recursion Desired bit clear, or that is not configured for recursion for a domain for which it is not authoritative, and for a resolver that receives a query with the RD bit clear.

Code 21, Not Supported, means the requested operation or query is not supported. Code 22, No Reachable Authority, means the resolver could not reach any of the authoritative name servers, or they potentially refused to reply. Code 23, Network Error, means an unrecoverable error occurred while communicating with another server. Code 24, Invalid Data, means the authoritative server cannot answer with data for a zone it is otherwise configured to support, for example because its most recent zone is too old or has expired.
sections.plainLanguage: The 25 codes fall into a few families. A validation failure has its own set of codes, one for each way DNSSEC can fail, so an operator can tell a missing DNSKEY from an expired signature. A block gets three codes depending on who imposed it: the operator, an outside authority, or the client. And there are operational codes for a server that was not ready, could not reach the authority, or holds data that is too old.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
A new EDNS0 option is defined, entitled Extended DNS Error, with the assigned value 15 from the DNS EDNS0 Option Codes registry, with status Standard.

A new registry is created and maintained, called Extended DNS Error Codes, on the Domain Name System Parameters page. The range 0 to 49151 is First Come First Served, and the range 49152 to 65535 is Private Use. The registry is a table with three columns, INFO-CODE, Purpose and Reference, and its initial content is the 25 codes defined in the document, with the range 25 to 49151 unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: One new option number is reserved for the mechanism, and a new registry is created for the error codes, with the upper half left for private use so that an organisation can use its own codes without touching the shared list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Although DNSSEC continues to be deployed, a significant number of clients, around 11% according to the cited survey, that receive a SERVFAIL from a validating resolver because of a DNSSEC validation issue will simply ask the next, potentially non-validating, resolver in their list, and thus do not get the protections DNSSEC should provide.

EDE information is unauthenticated unless secured by a form of secured DNS transaction, such as TSIG, SIG(0), DNS over DTLS or DNS over HTTPS. An attacker, for example a man in the middle or a malicious recursive server, could insert an extended error response into untrusted data, although ideally clients and resolvers would not trust any unauthenticated information. EDE content should be treated only as diagnostic information and must not alter DNS protocol processing. Until all DNS answers are authenticated, there are trade-offs: an attacker able to insert the DNSSEC Bogus error into a DNS message could instead simply reply with a fictitious address record. Note that DNS RCODEs also contain no authentication and can be just as easily manipulated.

By design, EDE potentially exposes additional information through the DNS resolution process that may leak information. An example is the Prohibited code, which may leak the fact that a name is on a blocklist.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra information is not authenticated, so anyone who can tamper with DNS traffic could put a false reason in it. That is why it must never change how a query is answered: a liar gains nothing by adding a note to a response, because the real response code still says what happened. A second point is that a blocklist reason can itself be a leak, since it tells an observer that a name was listed.

items.title: DNSSEC validation
items.text: Codes 1, 2 and 5 to 12: the resolver tried to validate the answer and could not.

items.title: Policy and blocking
items.text: Codes 15, 16, 17 and 18: the name is on a blocklist imposed by the operator, by an outside authority, or by the client.

items.title: Operational problems
items.text: Codes 14, 21, 22, 23 and 24: the server was not ready, the operation is not supported, no authority could be reached, a network error occurred, or the data is too old.

items.title: Cache and stale answers
items.text: Codes 3, 13 and 19: the resolver answered from its cache because it could not get a fresh answer.
